summary: Describes a protocol for configuring SSH public keys in an implementation-independent way. SSH authenticates users by public key but defined no mechanism to distribute them, and no common solution exists.

plainLanguage.summary: SSH can log you in with a public key, but it says nothing about how that key gets onto the server. Each program has its own way of doing it. This document defines one small service, called a subsystem, that lets an already logged-in client add, remove and list the user's own keys the same way everywhere.

subtitle: A small SSH subsystem that lets a logged-in user add, remove and list their own public keys on a server.

tldr.problem: SSH can authenticate a user with a public key but defines no way to get that key onto the server, so every implementation does it differently.
tldr.mechanism: A subsystem named publickey runs inside an authenticated SSH session and offers four operations: add, remove, list and listattributes, with optional attributes that restrict how a key may be used.
tldr.outcome: Client software can manage a user's keys the same way on any server that implements the subsystem. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9519.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol for secure remote login and other secure network services over an insecure network. Secure Shell defines a user authentication mechanism that is based on public keys, but does not define any mechanism for key distribution. Common practice is to authenticate once with password authentication and transfer the public key to the server. To date, no two implementations use the same mechanism to configure a public key for use.

This document describes a subsystem that can be used to configure public keys in an implementation-independent fashion, which allows client software to take on the burden of this configuration. The protocol is designed for extreme simplicity in implementation, and is not intended as a Public Key Infrastructure for X.509 Certificates replacement.

The Secure Shell Public Key Subsystem has been designed to run on top of the Secure Shell transport layer and user authentication protocols. It provides a simple mechanism for the client to manage public keys on the server. It is intended to be used from the Secure Shell Connection Protocol as a subsystem, as described in the section on starting a shell or a command. The subsystem name used with this protocol is publickey.

The protocol requires that the user be able to authenticate in some fashion before it can be used. If password authentication is used, servers SHOULD provide a configuration option to disable the use of password authentication after the first public key is added.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH can log you in with a public key, but it says nothing about how that key gets onto the server. Each program has its own way of doing it. This document defines one small service, called a subsystem, that lets an already logged-in client add, remove and list the user's own keys the same way everywhere.

sections.title: Opening the Public Key Subsystem
sections.content:
The Public Key Subsystem is started by a client sending an SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST over an existing session's channel. The request carries the recipient channel, the string subsystem, a flag asking for a reply, and the string publickey. Client implementations SHOULD reject this request, because it is normally sent only by the client.

If the want reply flag is TRUE, the server MUST respond with SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_SUCCESS if the Public Key Subsystem was successfully started, or SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE if the server failed to start it or does not support it. The server SHOULD respond with SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE if the user is not allowed access to the Public Key Subsystem, for example because the user authenticated with a restricted public key. It is RECOMMENDED that clients request and check the reply for this request.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens the subsystem by asking the server to start a service named publickey on the session channel it already has. The server answers with success or failure, and a failure is the right answer if the server does not offer the service or the user's key is too restricted to use it.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Status Messages
sections.content:
All requests and responses take the same shape: a length, a name, and then data specific to the request or the response. The length field describes the length of the name field and of the request-specific data, but does not include the length of the length field itself. The client MUST receive acknowledgement of each request prior to sending a new request.

A request is acknowledged by sending a status packet, which carries a status code, a description and a language tag. If there is data in response to the request, the status packet is sent after all the data has been sent. A status message MUST be sent for any unrecognized packet, and the request SHOULD NOT close the subsystem.

The status code gives the status in a machine-readable format suitable for localization. Ten values are defined: SSH_PUBLICKEY_SUCCESS, 0; SSH_PUBLICKEY_ACCESS_DENIED, 1; SSH_PUBLICKEY_STORAGE_EXCEEDED, 2; SSH_PUBLICKEY_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED, 3; SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_NOT_FOUND, 4; SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_NOT_SUPPORTED, 5; SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_ALREADY_PRESENT, 6; SSH_PUBLICKEY_GENERAL_FAILURE, 7; SSH_PUBLICKEY_REQUEST_NOT_SUPPORTED, 8; and SSH_PUBLICKEY_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED, 9. If a request completed successfully, the server MUST send SSH_PUBLICKEY_SUCCESS.

The request names registered by IANA are version, add, remove, list and listattributes, and the response names are version, status, publickey and attribute. All registered names MUST be printable US-ASCII strings, MUST NOT contain the at-sign, a comma, or whitespace or control characters, are case-sensitive, and MUST NOT be longer than 64 characters. The IANA does not register or control names containing an at-sign, which have the format name@domainname.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a name and a length, and the server always finishes with a status message that says what happened. There are ten status codes, from 0 for success to 9 for an attribute the server does not support.

sections.title: The Version Packet
sections.content:
Both sides MUST start a connection by sending a version packet that indicates the version of the protocol they are using. This document describes version 2 of the protocol; version 1 was used by an early draft of this document, and the version number was incremented after changes in the handling of status packets.

Both sides send the highest version that they implement, and the lower of the two version numbers is the version of the protocol to use. If either side cannot support the lower version, it should close the subsystem and notify the other side by sending an SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_CLOSE message. Before closing the subsystem, a status message with the status SSH_PUBLICKEY_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED SHOULD be sent. This is normally the only occasion on which the client sends a status message, since normally status messages are sent by the server in response to requests.

Both sides MUST wait to receive this version before continuing, and the version packet MUST NOT be sent again after this initial exchange. The SSH_PUBLICKEY_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED status code must not be sent in response to any other request. Implementations MAY use the first 15 bytes of the version packet as a magic cookie, to avoid processing spurious output from the user's shell. Those bytes are always the same.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else, both sides send a version packet. Each sends the highest version it understands, and the lower of the two wins. If one side cannot do that, it says so and closes the channel.

sections.title: Adding and Removing a Public Key
sections.content:
To add a key the client sends an add request holding the public key algorithm name, the public key blob, an overwrite flag, and a count of attributes followed by that many attribute name and value pairs with a critical flag each. The format of the public key blob is detailed in the SSH Transport Protocol document.

The server MUST attempt to store the public key for the user in the appropriate location, so the public key can be used for subsequent public key authentications. If the overwrite field is false and the specified key already exists, the server MUST return SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_ALREADY_PRESENT, and the client SHOULD then provide an option to the user to overwrite the key. If the overwrite field is true and the specified key already exists but cannot be overwritten, the server MUST return SSH_PUBLICKEY_ACCESS_DENIED.

Attribute names are defined following the same scheme laid out for algorithm names in the SSH protocol architecture. If the server does not implement a critical attribute, it MUST fail the add, with the status code SSH_PUBLICKEY_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED. For the purposes of a critical attribute, mere storage of the attribute is not sufficient: the server must understand and implement the intent of the attribute.

Removing a key uses a remove request holding just the algorithm name and the key blob. The server MUST attempt to remove the public key for the user from the appropriate location, so that the public key cannot be used for subsequent authentications.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a key sends the key's algorithm name and its bytes, an overwrite flag, and any attributes that come with it. If the key is already there and overwriting was not asked for, the server says so and the client can ask the user. If a critical attribute is one the server does not implement, the add fails rather than being silently weakened.

sections.title: Key Attributes and Restrictions
sections.content:
Attributes define properties or restrictions for public keys, and thirteen are defined in this document. The comment attribute holds user-specified text about the key, which the server SHOULD preserve and return with the key during any subsequent list operation, and which the server MUST NOT attempt to interpret or act upon in any way. It must be in UTF-8, and it SHOULD NOT be critical, so that the user can identify the key without resorting to comparing its fingerprint. The comment-language attribute specifies the language of the preceding comment, MUST immediately follow a comment attribute, and lets the client give more than one comment with a different language for each.

Several attributes restrict what may happen when the key is used. command-override specifies a command to be executed when the key is in use, in place of the command or shell which would otherwise have been executed as a result of the request. If the command string is empty, both exec and shell requests should be denied, and if no command-override attribute is specified, all exec and shell requests should be permitted, as long as they satisfy other security or authorization checks the server may perform. subsystem specifies a comma-separated list of subsystems that may be started when this key is in use; if the value is empty, no subsystems may be started, and if the attribute is not specified, no restriction is placed on which subsystems may be started.

Five attributes deny one kind of request: shell denies session channel shell requests, exec denies exec requests, env denies env requests, agent denies auth-agent-req requests, and x11 specifies that X11 forwarding may not be performed. For each of these the attribute value field SHOULD be empty. All of these SHOULD be critical.

Two attributes limit where the key may be used and what it may reach. from specifies a comma-separated list of hosts from which the key may be used, and an authorization attempt from a host not in that list MUST be denied, with the server SHOULD making a log entry about it. The server MAY provide a method for administrators to disallow the appearance of a host in this list, and should use whatever method is appropriate for its platform to identify the host, such as checking the IP address or performing a reverse DNS lookup. port-forward specifies that no direct-tcpip requests should be accepted, except those to hosts in the comma-separated list it holds, and an empty value refuses them all. reverse-forward does the same for tcpip-forward requests and the port numbers in its list.

In addition to the attributes specified by the client, the server MAY provide a method for administrators to enforce certain attributes compulsorily.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key can carry attributes that describe it or limit what it may do. A comment lets the user recognise a key. The command-override, subsystem and from attributes decide what the key may run and where it may be used from. The shell, exec, env, agent and x11 attributes each refuse one kind of request, and the two forward attributes limit which hosts and ports the key can reach.

sections.title: Listing Keys and Server Capabilities
sections.content:
To list the known public keys the client sends a list request. The server responds with zero or more publickey responses, each holding the algorithm name, the key blob and the key's attributes, and then a status packet. There is no requirement that the responses be in any particular order, and client implementations should not rely on responses being in any order. Implementations SHOULD support this request.

To find out which key attributes the server supports, the client sends a listattributes request. The server responds with zero or more attribute responses, each holding an attribute name and a compulsory flag. The compulsory field indicates whether the attribute will be compulsorily applied to any added keys, irrespective of whether the client specified it, because of administrative settings on the server. If the server does not support administrative settings of this nature, it MUST return false in the compulsory field. The example given in the RFC is a server whose configuration file says the user is not permitted shell access: the server returns the shell attribute with compulsory marked true, and applies it whatever the user subsequently asks for, rendering it impossible for the user to use a shell.

After the last attribute response, a status packet MUST be sent. An implementation MAY choose not to support this request.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more requests read back information. The list request returns every key the server holds for the user, with its attributes, followed by a status message. The listattributes request returns the attributes the server understands, and marks as compulsory the ones it will apply on its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This protocol assumes that it is run over a secure channel and that the endpoints of the channel have been authenticated. Thus, this protocol assumes that it is externally protected from network-level attacks.

The protocol provides a mechanism that allows client authentication data to be uploaded and manipulated. It is the responsibility of the server implementation to enforce any access controls that may be required to limit the access allowed for any particular user, the user being authenticated externally to this protocol. In particular, it is possible for users to overwrite an existing key on the server with this protocol, while at the same time specifying fewer restrictions for the new key than were previously present. Servers should take care that clients are not able to override presets from the server's administrator.

The protocol requires the client to assume that the server will correctly implement and observe attributes applied to keys. Implementation errors in the server could cause clients to authorize keys for access they were not intended to have, or to apply fewer restrictions than were intended.
sections.plainLanguage: The subsystem is only as safe as the SSH session it runs in, so it assumes an authenticated, protected channel. The server has to enforce the rules: a client can replace a key and ask for fewer restrictions, so the server must not let that override what the administrator set. Clients also have to trust the server to honour the restrictions on each key.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_STORAGE_EXCEEDED
items.desc: There is no room left to store the key.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The two sides could not agree on a protocol version.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_NOT_FOUND
items.desc: The key is not known to the server.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The server does not support that key algorithm.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_ALREADY_PRESENT
items.desc: The key is already stored and overwrite was not requested.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_REQUEST_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: The server does not implement that request.

items.label: SSH_PUBLICKEY_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: A critical attribute is not implemented by the server.

items.title: comment
items.text: Free text stored with the key so the user can recognise it.

items.title: command-override
items.text: Runs this command instead of the shell or command the client asked for.

items.title: subsystem
items.text: The comma-separated list of subsystems that may be started with this key.

items.title: from
items.text: The hosts this key may be used from; any other host is refused.

items.title: port-forward
items.text: The hosts that direct-tcpip forwarding is allowed to reach.

items.title: reverse-forward
items.text: The ports that tcpip-forward requests are allowed to bind.

items.title: shell, exec, env, agent, x11
items.text: Each one denies that kind of request when the key is used.
